questions.text: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding erectile dysfunction?
options: PDE-5 inhibitors can be given safely together with nitrate medications
The dorsal penile/pudendal nerves carry efferent (motor) fibers arising from S2–S4
Afferent sensory information travels from the penile ischiocavernosus/bulbocavernosus muscles to Onuf's nucleus
A man with preserved nocturnal erections who cannot achieve erection for intercourse is likely to have a psychogenic cause
There is no role for checking serum glucose and lipid profile in the evaluation of ED

The dorsal penile/pudendal nerves carry efferent (motor) fibers arising from S2–S4

questions.correctAnswer: D) A man with preserved nocturnal erections who cannot achieve erection for intercourse is likely to have a psychogenic cause
questions.correctAnswerText: A man with preserved nocturnal erections who cannot achieve erection for intercourse is likely to have a psychogenic cause
questions.explanation: Preserved nocturnal penile tumescence indicates intact vascular and neurological pathways, so failure only during intercourse points to a psychogenic cause; B and C reverse the true afferent/efferent relationships, and A and E are simply false.

questions.text: Tumescence (the erectile phase) is mediated by:
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic fibers from S2–S4 release nitric oxide, which raises cGMP and relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle, producing tumescence; sympathetic (thoracolumbar) outflow instead causes detumescence.

questions.text: All of the following are possible causes of non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism EXCEPT:
options: Needle injury to the cavernosal artery
originalOptions: Needle injury to the cavernosal artery
questions.explanation: Non-ischemic priapism results from an arterio-sinusoidal fistula, classically from trauma, needle injury, or iatrogenic penile surgery; neurologic shock is instead a recognized cause of ischemic (low-flow) priapism.

questions.text: Regarding priapism, which of the following statements is correct?
options: It results in impotence if left untreated beyond a critical duration of prolonged ischemia
It is only seen following intracavernosal injections
It is best diagnosed by a plain lateral X-ray of the pelvis
It is more commonly caused by Alprostadil than by Papaverine
It may be treated by saphenofemoral shunting alone as first-line therapy
originalOptions: It results in impotence if left untreated beyond a critical duration of prolonged ischemia
It is only seen following intracavernosal injections
It is best diagnosed by a plain lateral X-ray of the pelvis
It is more commonly caused by Alprostadil than by Papaverine
It may be treated by saphenofemoral shunting alone as first-line therapy
questions.correctAnswer: A) It results in impotence if left untreated beyond a critical duration of prolonged ischemia
questions.correctAnswerText: It results in impotence if left untreated beyond a critical duration of prolonged ischemia
questions.explanation: Prolonged ischemic priapism causes progressive corporal fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction if not urgently treated; priapism has many causes besides injections, is diagnosed by aspiration/blood gas and Doppler (not plain X-ray), and shunting is a later, not first-line, option.

questions.text: Which condition is characteristically associated with subcutaneous wire/device erosion through the skin?
questions.explanation: Erosion of the implanted device or its components through the overlying skin is a recognized mechanical complication of penile prosthesis surgery.

questions.text: Which of the following antihypertensive drugs negatively affects erectile function?
questions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics (Hydrochlorothiazide) are reported to cause ED, while alpha-blockers (terazosin) and ARBs (losartan) tend to improve sexual function, and amlodipine/captopril are not associated with worsening erectile function.

questions.text: Which characteristic is typically associated with organic ED, in contrast to psychogenic ED?
options: Presence of an identifiable interpersonal relationship factor
originalOptions: Presence of an identifiable interpersonal relationship factor
questions.correctAnswer: A) Gradual decline in erectile ability
questions.explanation: Organic ED typically has a progressive, gradual course, whereas sudden onset, situational occurrence, and preserved morning/nocturnal erections all favor a psychogenic cause.

questions.text: During a rigid erection, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: Dilation of the arterioles and arteries
Subtunical venous compression reducing venous outflow
Corporal pressure rises to several hundred millimeters of mercury
originalOptions: Dilation of the arterioles and arteries
Subtunical venous compression reducing venous outflow
Corporal pressure rises to several hundred millimeters of mercury
questions.correctAnswer: C) Relaxation of the ischiocavernosus muscles
questions.explanation: The ischiocavernosus muscles actively contract (not relax) during the rigid erection phase, compressing the crura and driving intracorporal pressure well above systolic blood pressure.

questions.text: A quadriplegic patient presents with priapism. Corporeal blood gas analysis reveals PO2 = 94, PCO2 = 37, pH = 7.4. He was previously treated with intracavernosal phenylephrine without improvement. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.explanation: A near-normal blood gas indicates non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism, which is managed conservatively and, if intervention is required, by selective arterial embolization rather than aspiration or agents used for ischemic priapism.

questions.text: In ischemic priapism, which of the following is typically absent?
questions.explanation: Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is characterized by absent or markedly reduced arterial inflow to the cavernosal artery on Doppler, with a painful, fully rigid erection.

questions.text: Which of the following is a psychogenic cause of erectile dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Anxiety acts through overinhibition of the spinal erection center and excessive sympathetic outflow, making it a psychogenic cause, while the other options are organic/structural causes of ED.

questions.text: Pain in the flaccid penis is usually due to:
options: A calculus impacted in the distal ureter
originalOptions: A calculus impacted in the distal ureter
questions.explanation: Pain in the flaccid penis typically reflects bladder or urethral inflammation (or paraphimosis), whereas Peyronie's disease and priapism classically cause pain in the erect penis.

questions.text: All of the following are characteristics of psychogenic ED EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A gradual, progressive decline in erectile function is characteristic of organic ED, whereas sudden onset, situational occurrence, and preserved nocturnal erections point to a psychogenic cause.

questions.text: What will penile Doppler ultrasound show in a case of ischemic priapism?
options: Increased venous outflow from the corpora
Increased arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
originalOptions: Increased venous outflow from the corpora
Increased arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
questions.correctAnswer: D) Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
questions.correctAnswerText: Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
questions.explanation: Ischemic priapism is a low-flow state, so Doppler characteristically shows absent or minimal arterial inflow into the cavernosal artery.

questions.text: A patient presents with priapism of 2 weeks' duration; corporeal blood gas shows PO2 > 90, PCO2 < 30. What is the best management?
questions.explanation: A high PO2 and low PCO2 indicate non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism, which, when intervention is required, is managed with selective arterial embolization rather than aspiration or sympathomimetic injection, which are used for ischemic priapism.

questions.text: An 80-year-old paraplegic man develops a prolonged, painful erection after an intracorporeal injection given to treat erectile dysfunction. Which intracorporeal drug should be given to relieve him?
questions.explanation: This describes ischemic priapism following intracavernosal injection therapy, which is treated with aspiration/irrigation followed by intracavernosal phenylephrine (an alpha-agonist); alprostadil, papaverine, and sildenafil are used to induce erection, not to treat priapism.

questions.text: A 38-year-old paraplegic man develops a sustained erection lasting 10 hours following intracorporeal injection of 10 mcg of prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil). What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: This is drug-induced ischemic priapism, which is treated with corporal aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine, an alpha-agonist that induces vasoconstriction and detumescence.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors is TRUE?
options: Sildenafil has efficacy maintained for approximately 4–6 hours
They increase the cytoplasmic concentration of cAMP
They can be safely combined with nitrates
Tadalafil has a shorter duration of action than sildenafil

They increase the cytoplasmic concentration of cAMP
They can be safely combined with nitrates
Tadalafil has a shorter duration of action than sildenafil
questions.correctAnswer: A) Sildenafil has efficacy maintained for approximately 4–6 hours
questions.correctAnswerText: Sildenafil has efficacy maintained for approximately 4–6 hours
questions.explanation: Sildenafil and vardenafil act within 30–60 minutes with efficacy maintained for about 4–6 hours, unlike tadalafil which lasts up to 36 hours; PDE5 inhibitors raise cGMP (not cAMP) and are contraindicated with nitrates.

questions.text: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors increase the cytoplasmic concentration of:
questions.explanation: PDE5 inhibitors block the breakdown of cGMP by phosphodiesterase type 5, prolonging cGMP-mediated cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation.

questions.text: An elderly patient on nitroglycerin presents with erectile dysfunction. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrate use due to the risk of severe hypotension, so a non-pharmacologic option such as a vacuum erection device is appropriate; testosterone and tamsulosin are not indicated without evidence of hypogonadism or BPH.

questions.text: All of the following favor a diagnosis of organic (rather than psychogenic) erectile dysfunction EXCEPT:
options: Gradual, progressive decline in erectile function
Persistent difficulty in all sexual situations

questions.explanation: Preserved morning/nocturnal erections with failure only during intercourse indicates intact erectile machinery and points to a psychogenic cause, whereas the other options describe the persistent, progressive, NPTR-abnormal pattern typical of organic ED.

questions.correctAnswerText: Arteriogenic ED — decreased peak systolic velocity; Venogenic ED — persistent end-diastolic flow
questions.explanation: Arteriogenic ED reflects reduced arterial inflow, shown as a low peak systolic velocity, while venogenic ED reflects failure of veno-occlusion, shown as persistent end-diastolic flow despite adequate inflow.

questions.text: Which of the following is correct? [img: ABtrue.png]

Both A and B are false

questions.correctAnswer: C) Both A and B are true
questions.correctAnswerText: Both A and B are true
questions.explanation: Arterial ED impairs the ability to "get" an erection due to insufficient inflow, while venous (venogenic) ED impairs the ability to "keep" an erection because blood escapes despite adequate inflow — both statements are correct.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized hormonal cause of erectile dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Both hypogonadism (low testosterone) and hyperprolactinemia are established hormonal causes of ED; hyperprolactinemia additionally suppresses GnRH, which further lowers testosterone.

questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of PDE5 inhibitors in the treatment of erectile dysfunction?
options: They increase cAMP by inhibiting adenylate cyclase breakdown
They directly stimulate nitric oxide synthase
They prevent breakdown of cGMP, prolonging cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation
They block alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in the prostate and bladder neck
originalOptions: They increase cAMP by inhibiting adenylate cyclase breakdown
They directly stimulate nitric oxide synthase
They prevent breakdown of cGMP, prolonging cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation
They block alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in the prostate and bladder neck
questions.correctAnswer: C) They prevent breakdown of cGMP, prolonging cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation
questions.correctAnswerText: They prevent breakdown of cGMP, prolonging cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation
questions.explanation: Sexual stimulation triggers NO release, raising cGMP; PDE5 inhibitors block the enzyme that degrades cGMP, thereby prolonging smooth muscle relaxation and erection — they require intact sexual stimulation and do not act independently.

questions.text: All of the following are true regarding contraindications and adverse effects of PDE5 inhibitors EXCEPT:
options: They are contraindicated with nitrate/NO-donor use due to risk of severe hypotension
They are contraindicated with guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat
Common adverse effects include headache and flushing

They are contraindicated with guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat
Common adverse effects include headache and flushing

questions.correctAnswer: D) They can be safely co-administered with nitroglycerin in patients with stable angina
questions.correctAnswerText: They can be safely co-administered with nitroglycerin in patients with stable angina
questions.explanation: Combining PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates or guanylate cyclase stimulators can precipitate severe, refractory hypotension and is absolutely contraindicated; headache and flushing are recognized common side effects.

questions.explanation: Sildenafil's characteristic adverse effect is visual disturbance (related to PDE6 cross-reactivity in the retina), while tadalafil is notably associated with back pain and myalgia.

questions.correctAnswerText: First: lifestyle correction + PDE5 inhibitor; Second: intracavernosal injection/vacuum device; Third: penile prosthesis
questions.explanation: The traditional exam-based hierarchy is lifestyle modification with a PDE5 inhibitor (± psychosexual therapy) as first-line, intracavernosal injection or vacuum erection device as second-line, and penile prosthesis reserved as third-line for treatment failures.

options: A persistent penile erection unrelated to sexual stimulation that fails to subside

A transient erection occurring only with intracavernosal injection
questions.correctAnswer: A) A persistent penile erection unrelated to sexual stimulation that fails to subside
questions.correctAnswerText: A persistent penile erection unrelated to sexual stimulation that fails to subside
questions.explanation: Priapism is defined as a prolonged erection that continues independent of, or beyond, sexual stimulation and does not resolve spontaneously, classically lasting at least 4 hours.

questions.text: Which combination correctly pairs a cause with its associated type of priapism?
options: Sickle cell disease — non-ischemic priapism; Blunt perineal trauma — ischemic priapism

Sickle cell disease — ischemic priapism; Cavernosal arterial injury — non-ischemic priapism

Sickle cell disease — ischemic priapism; Cavernosal arterial injury — non-ischemic priapism
questions.correctAnswer: D) Sickle cell disease — ischemic priapism; Cavernosal arterial injury — non-ischemic priapism
questions.correctAnswerText: Sickle cell disease — ischemic priapism; Cavernosal arterial injury — non-ischemic priapism
questions.explanation: Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is classically caused by sickle cell disease and vasoactive/intracavernosal drugs, while non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism results from blunt perineal or penile trauma causing a cavernosal arterial injury (arteriocavernosal fistula).

options: Ischemic priapism is painful; non-ischemic priapism is usually painless
Ischemic priapism shows dark, hypoxic, hypercarbic, acidotic cavernosal blood; non-ischemic shows bright, arterial-type blood
Ischemic priapism is fully rigid; non-ischemic priapism is only partially rigid
Ischemic priapism is a true urological emergency requiring urgent treatment
Non-ischemic priapism is typically associated with sickle cell disease rather than trauma

questions.explanation: Non-ischemic priapism is associated with perineal/penile trauma, not sickle cell disease, which is instead a classic cause of ischemic priapism; all the other listed distinctions (pain, blood gas, rigidity, emergency status) are accurate.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly identifies two intracavernosal drugs used for erectile dysfunction and a shared major adverse effect?
options: Alprostadil and papaverine — priapism and penile fibrosis
originalOptions: Alprostadil and papaverine — priapism and penile fibrosis
questions.correctAnswer: C) Alprostadil and papaverine — priapism and penile fibrosis
questions.correctAnswerText: Alprostadil and papaverine — priapism and penile fibrosis
questions.explanation: Alprostadil (PGE1) and papaverine are the classic intracavernosal injection agents for ED, and both carry the risk of priapism and penile fibrosis with repeated use; sildenafil/tadalafil are oral agents, phenylephrine/phentolamine are used to treat priapism, and testosterone/finasteride are hormonal/systemic therapies, not intracavernosal drugs.

questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes true hematuria from hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria?
questions.explanation: Dipstick is positive for blood in all three conditions, but only true hematuria shows intact red blood cells on microscopic urinalysis.

questions.text: A patient reports blood appearing only at the very end of the urinary stream, after most of the urine has already passed. This pattern of terminal hematuria most suggests pathology arising from:
questions.correctAnswer: A) Bladder neck or prostatic inflammation
questions.explanation: Initial hematuria localizes to the urethra, total hematuria to the bladder or upper tract, and terminal hematuria to the bladder neck or prostatic urethra.

questions.text: A 68-year-old smoker presents with a single episode of painless gross hematuria. Which diagnosis must be excluded first as the classic cause of painless gross hematuria in a patient over 50 years old?
questions.explanation: Painless gross hematuria in a patient over 50 is bladder cancer until proven otherwise, warranting cystoscopy and upper tract imaging regardless of other findings.

questions.text: A normotensive patient is found to have isolated microscopic hematuria on routine urinalysis, with no other urinary symptoms and a normal examination. What is the most appropriate initial action?
questions.explanation: Isolated, asymptomatic microscopic hematuria in a low-risk patient is initially managed conservatively with a repeat urinalysis rather than immediate invasive workup.

questions.text: When taking a history from a patient presenting with hematuria, which combination of questions is most important to ask?
questions.explanation: Onset, presence of clots, and timing during the urinary stream all help localize the source and severity of hematuria, so all should be asked.

questions.text: Hematuria in an adult should be treated as a warning sign of which of the following until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: Although hematuria has many causes, it is classically taught that hematuria in an adult signals malignancy, most often bladder cancer, until excluded.

questions.text: A 70-year-old male smoker presents with gross hematuria persisting for 3 months. What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
questions.explanation: Persistent gross hematuria in an older smoker requires full evaluation of both the upper tract (CT urogram) and lower tract (cystoscopy) to exclude urothelial malignancy.

questions.text: Which of the following best defines stress urinary incontinence?
options: Involuntary leakage preceded by a sudden urge to void
Continuous leakage of urine unrelated to activity
Leakage of urine that occurs only during sleep
Leakage of urine following bladder overdistension
Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing
originalOptions: Involuntary leakage preceded by a sudden urge to void
Continuous leakage of urine unrelated to activity
Leakage of urine that occurs only during sleep
Leakage of urine following bladder overdistension
Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing
questions.correctAnswer: E) Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing
questions.correctAnswerText: Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing
questions.explanation: Stress incontinence occurs when rises in intra-abdominal pressure overcome urethral resistance, typically from pelvic floor weakness or sphincteric incompetence.

questions.text: A patient with overactive bladder and urgency incontinence is being started on treatment. Which type of incontinence is most often managed pharmacologically as first-line therapy?
questions.explanation: Urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity responds well to antimuscarinics or beta-3 agonists (mirabegron), unlike stress incontinence, which is managed primarily with conservative or surgical measures.

questions.text: A 48-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presents with urine leakage on coughing and sneezing. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.explanation: Conservative pelvic floor exercises (at least 8 contractions, 3 times daily for 3 months) are first-line before considering surgical options such as slings or Burch colposuspension.

questions.text: A 43-year-old woman develops constant urinary leakage 7 days after hysterectomy, not aggravated by coughing and without associated urgency. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.explanation: Continuous, position-independent leakage after pelvic surgery strongly suggests an iatrogenic vesicovaginal fistula creating a direct communication between bladder and vagina.

questions.text: Continuous incontinence, defined as leakage of urine at all times and in all positions, is most commonly caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation: A fistulous communication between the bladder and vagina bypasses the normal continence mechanism entirely, producing constant leakage regardless of posture or activity.

questions.text: In female patients, an ectopic ureter classically causes continuous urinary incontinence because the ureter inserts:
options: Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
originalOptions: Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
questions.correctAnswer: A) Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
questions.correctAnswerText: Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
questions.explanation: In females, an ectopic ureter frequently opens below the external sphincter, bypassing continence mechanisms; in males it opens above the sphincter and instead causes recurrent UTIs rather than incontinence.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT considered a risk factor for urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation: Female sex, not male sex, is a recognized risk factor for urinary incontinence due to a shorter urethra and the effects of pregnancy and childbirth on pelvic floor support.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor specifically for stress urinary incontinence?
questions.explanation: Vaginal childbirth weakens pelvic floor support and increases SUI risk, whereas nulliparous women have a comparatively lower risk.

questions.text: Which class of medication should be avoided when treating stress urinary incontinence in a male patient?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics target detrusor overactivity in urge incontinence and have no role in stress incontinence, which in men is usually secondary to sphincter injury after prostate surgery.

questions.text: What is the most common overall indication for placement of an indwelling Foley catheter?
options: Drainage of acute or chronic urinary retention
originalOptions: Drainage of acute or chronic urinary retention
questions.correctAnswer: B) Drainage of acute or chronic urinary retention
questions.correctAnswerText: Drainage of acute or chronic urinary retention
questions.explanation: Drainage of acute or chronic retention (or post-void residual) is the most common indication for catheterization; monitoring urine output is the second most common.

questions.text: A patient started on an antimuscarinic for urge incontinence develops several adverse effects. Which of the following is NOT typically caused by anticholinergic medications?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation, not diarrhea, along with dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, and confusion.

questions.text: Before initiating mirabegron for urge incontinence, which of the following should prompt the greatest caution or avoidance of therapy?
questions.explanation: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure, so severe uncontrolled hypertension is a major safety concern, whereas significant urinary retention with high PVR is a relative caution rather than the primary contraindication.

questions.text: During cystometry, a patient's intravesical pressure (Pves) is 45 cmH2O and abdominal pressure (Pabd) is 15 cmH2O. What is the calculated detrusor pressure (Pdet)?
questions.explanation: Detrusor pressure is calculated as Pdet = Pves − Pabd, so 45 − 15 = 30 cmH2O.

questions.text: A 6-year-old child is undergoing urodynamic evaluation. Using the standard pediatric formula, what is the expected bladder capacity?
questions.explanation: Pediatric bladder capacity is estimated as (Age + 2) × 30 mL; for a 6-year-old this is (6+2) × 30 = 240 mL.

questions.text: Before initiating mirabegron for the treatment of urge urinary incontinence, which of the following conditions is the most appropriate reason to avoid or use the drug with significant caution?
options: Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual
originalOptions: Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual
questions.correctAnswer: B) Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual
questions.correctAnswerText: Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual
questions.explanation: Mirabegron (a β3-adrenergic agonist) relaxes the detrusor muscle during bladder filling, which may worsen pre-existing urinary retention. Therefore, patients with significant urinary retention and a high post-void residual should generally avoid the drug or receive it only with careful monitoring. Dysuria, kidney stones, and hematuria are not contraindications by themselves.

questions.text: Which of the following syndromes represents the most common chromosomal cause of male infertility?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common chromosomal abnormality causing male infertility by leading to primary testicular failure and azoospermia, whereas Kallmann syndrome is a genetic hormone disorder (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) rather than a chromosomal aneuploidy, Turner syndrome exclusively affects females (45,X), and Noonan syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic condition not characterized by a chromosomal number defect.

questions.text: What is the first-line investigation of choice for a male presenting with infertility?
questions.explanation: Semen analysis (seminal fluid analysis) is the first-line investigation in male infertility, assessing volume, sperm concentration, motility, and morphology; hormonal testing, ultrasound, and karyotyping are reserved for further work-up based on initial findings.

questions.text: Infertility in males with cystic fibrosis is most commonly caused by which of the following?
options: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
originalOptions: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
questions.correctAnswer: B) Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
questions.correctAnswerText: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
questions.explanation: CFTR gene mutations in cystic fibrosis lead to CBAVD; spermatogenesis is normal, but the resulting obstructive azoospermia causes infertility.

questions.text: Which of the following is the primary inhibitor of LH release from the anterior pituitary?
questions.explanation: Testosterone provides negative feedback on both the hypothalamus (↓GnRH) and pituitary (↓LH). Inhibin B, secreted by Sertoli cells, selectively inhibits FSH rather than LH.

questions.text: Oligospermia is best defined as:

A low sperm concentration below the reference threshold
An abnormal percentage of sperm forms on morphology

A low sperm concentration below the reference threshold

questions.explanation: Oligospermia: sperm count less than 15 x10⁶/mL , A: Asthenospermia , B: Azoospermia , D: Teratospermia .

questions.text: Teratospermia refers to which of the following semen abnormalities?
options: Absence of sperm in the ejaculate
originalOptions: Absence of sperm in the ejaculate
questions.explanation: Teratospermia: sperm morphology below the lower reference limit of normal forms (WHO lower limit ~4% normal forms) , A: Azoospermia , B: Asthenospermia , C: Oligospermia .

questions.text: The majority of seminal fluid volume is contributed by which structure?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles contribute the majority of seminal fluid volume, while the prostate contributes about 1/6, and sperm contribute only about 1%.

questions.text: At which life stages do the major physiological peaks of testosterone production occur in males?
options: Embryonic (fetal) development, the neonatal period, and puberty
originalOptions: Embryonic (fetal) development, the neonatal period, and puberty
questions.correctAnswer: D) Embryonic (fetal) development, the neonatal period, and puberty
questions.correctAnswerText: Embryonic (fetal) development, the neonatal period, and puberty
questions.explanation: Testosterone peaks at three distinct life stages: embryonic development, the first few months of neonatal life (mini-puberty), and puberty — driving prostatic and genital development at each stage.

questions.text: A young male bodybuilder using exogenous testosterone is most likely to experience which effect on his fertility?
options: Increased fertility due to higher androgen levels
Decreased fertility due to suppression of pituitary FSH and LH
Fertility effects depend only on the route of administration

questions.correctAnswerText: Decreased fertility due to suppression of pituitary FSH and LH
questions.explanation: Exogenous testosterone suppresses hypothalamic-pituitary GnRH/FSH/LH secretion via negative feedback, lowering intratesticular testosterone and impairing spermatogenesis, unlike endogenous testicular testosterone.

questions.text: A patient presents with infertility, small testes, azoospermia, and an elevated FSH level. This clinical picture is most consistent with which of the following?
questions.explanation: Small testes, azoospermia, and elevated FSH indicate primary testicular failure (which is synonymous with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) ; hypogonadotropic hypogonadism instead presents with low FSH/LH , and obstructive azoospermia typically has a normal FSH.

questions.text: In a patient with azoospermia, which hormone finding suggests an obstructive cause rather than testicular failure?
questions.explanation: Obstructive azoospermia typically shows a normal FSH because spermatogenesis is intact, whereas non-obstructive azoospermia (testicular failure) shows an elevated FSH due to loss of Sertoli cell inhibin feedback.

questions.text: The anatomical basis of the blood-testis barrier is formed by which of the following?
options: The basement membrane of the seminiferous tubule
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
originalOptions: The basement membrane of the seminiferous tubule
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
questions.correctAnswer: B) Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
questions.correctAnswerText: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
questions.explanation: Sertoli cells are linked by tight junctions that form the blood-testis barrier, creating an immunologically privileged compartment for developing sperm, which form only after puberty.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized complication of cryptorchidism?
questions.explanation: Cryptorchidism impairs fertility due to an unfavorable thermal environment for spermatogenesis; it also raises the risk of testicular (not bladder) cancer.

questions.text: What is the karyotype of Klinefelter syndrome?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is caused by an extra X chromosome (47,XXY), resulting in small firm testes, gynecomastia, tall stature, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with infertility.

questions.text: Infertility is defined as the failure of a couple to achieve pregnancy after which duration of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse?
questions.explanation: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse; shorter periods (3–6 months) are not sufficient to establish the diagnosis since most couples conceive within a year.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs correctly represents the prevalence of varicocele in the general male population versus in infertile men?
questions.explanation: Varicocele affects about 15% of the general male population but is found in roughly 35–40% of infertile men, and is even more common in men with secondary infertility.

questions.text: Which of the following is considered a favorable prognostic factor in male infertility?
options: Absence of previous pregnancy with the same partner
originalOptions: Absence of previous pregnancy with the same partner
questions.explanation: A shorter duration of infertility, younger female partner age, and a history of previous conception are all favorable prognostic factors; the opposite findings (long duration, older maternal age, no prior pregnancy) indicate a poorer prognosis.

questions.text: All of the following are recognized categories of causes of male infertility EXCEPT:
options: Testicular causes (e.g., varicocele, cryptorchidism, Klinefelter syndrome)
Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
originalOptions: Testicular causes (e.g., varicocele, cryptorchidism, Klinefelter syndrome)
Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
questions.correctAnswer: E) Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
questions.correctAnswerText: Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
questions.explanation: Male infertility is classified into pre-testicular, testicular, post-testicular, and idiopathic causes; a purely psychological category unrelated to organic pathology is not part of this recognized classification.

questions.text: All of the following are recognized causes of obstructive azoospermia EXCEPT:
options: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
originalOptions: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
questions.explanation: CBAVD, vasectomy, post-infectious epididymal obstruction, and ejaculatory duct obstruction are classic causes of obstructive azoospermia with preserved spermatogenesis; Klinefelter syndrome causes non-obstructive (testicular failure) azoospermia due to primary testicular failure, not obstruction.

Typical obstructive azoospermia shows no sperm with low semen volume; ejaculatory duct obstruction shows normal volume with normal fructose

Both typical obstructive azoospermia and ejaculatory duct obstruction show normal semen volume and normal fructose
Obstructive azoospermia is always associated with elevated FSH regardless of the level of obstruction

questions.text: Which of the following pairs represents andrological conditions correctly associated with varicocele?
questions.explanation: Varicocele is classically associated with male infertility (abnormal semen parameters) and testicular hypotrophy/atrophy due to impaired thermoregulation and venous stasis; the other listed pairings are unrelated conditions not causally linked to varicocele.

questions.text: A young infertile male undergoes karyotype analysis. Which of the following is the most common genetic cause of male infertility?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common sex chromosome abnormality and genetic cause of male infertility, presenting with small firm testes, azoospermia, and elevated FSH/LH with low testosterone.

questions.text: During TURP, a patient develops confusion, nausea, bradycardia, and hypertension near the end of a prolonged resection. Serum sodium is low. This is best explained by:
options: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
originalOptions: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
questions.correctAnswer: A) Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
questions.correctAnswerText: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
questions.explanation: TUR syndrome results from absorption of hypotonic irrigating solution through open venous sinuses during resection, causing hypervolemic hyponatremia with confusion, bradycardia, hypertension, and visual disturbances.

questions.text: Which factor is most associated with increased risk of TUR syndrome?
options: Use of bipolar resection with saline irrigation
originalOptions: Use of bipolar resection with saline irrigation
questions.correctAnswer: C) Resection time greater than 90 minutes
questions.explanation: TUR syndrome risk increases with resection times exceeding 90 minutes and is more common in older men; bipolar TURP performed under saline (isotonic) irrigation reduces this risk.

questions.text: A patient requires long-term indwelling catheterization. Compared to latex, silicone catheters are preferred because they:
options: Are only available in smaller sizes
originalOptions: Are only available in smaller sizes
questions.explanation: Silicone catheters induce less tissue inflammation than latex, making them preferable for long-term catheterization, despite latex being cheaper and more widely available.

questions.text: A 24 French Foley catheter has an outer diameter of approximately:
questions.explanation: Catheter French size divided by 3 gives the outer diameter in millimeters; 24 ÷ 3 = 8 mm.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized indication for urethral catheterization?
options: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
Suspected urethral injury with blood at the meatus
High-riding prostate on rectal exam after trauma
Pelvic fracture with suspected urethral disruption

Pelvic fracture with suspected urethral disruption

questions.correctAnswerText: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
questions.explanation: Monitoring urine output is a standard, common indication for catheterization. Suspected urethral injury (blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, pelvic fracture with urethral disruption) is a contraindication until imaging excludes injury.

questions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to transurethral Foley catheter placement?
options: Need for a clean urine sample
originalOptions: Need for a clean urine sample
questions.explanation: Suspected urethral injury is a contraindication to urethral catheterization; a retrograde urethrogram should be performed first, and a suprapubic catheter used if drainage is needed.

questions.text: Chronic urinary retention is best distinguished from acute retention by which feature?
options: Sudden onset of severe suprapubic pain
Rapid resolution with a single catheterization
originalOptions: Sudden onset of severe suprapubic pain
Rapid resolution with a single catheterization
questions.correctAnswer: B) Painless, palpable, and percussible bladder
questions.explanation: Chronic retention classically presents as a painless, palpable/percussible bladder due to gradual distension, in contrast to the painful presentation of acute retention.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man with ischemic heart disease presents with fever of 40°C, HR 125, BP 120/65, and suprapubic tenderness consistent with acute bacterial prostatitis with urinary retention. The most appropriate management is:
options: Transurethral catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission

Suprapubic catheterization, IV antibiotics, and admission
Immediate transurethral resection of the prostate

Immediate transurethral resection of the prostate

questions.explanation: In acute bacterial prostatitis, urethral catheterization and instrumentation are contraindicated due to risk of bacteremia; urinary retention should be managed with a suprapubic catheter along with IV antibiotics and admission.

questions.text: Which of the following clinical situations requires urgent decompression of the urinary tract?
options: A small asymptomatic stone with mild pain
originalOptions: A small asymptomatic stone with mild pain
questions.correctAnswer: C) An obstructed, infected collecting system
questions.explanation: An obstructed and infected urinary system (obstructive pyelonephritis/pyonephrosis) is a urologic emergency requiring urgent decompression via JJ stent or nephrostomy to prevent sepsis and renal destruction.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized complication of long-term double-J (JJ) ureteral stenting?
questions.explanation: Long-standing catheters (not JJ stents specifically) are linked to stone formation and bladder cancer risk with prolonged indwelling urethral catheters; urothelial cancer is not a typical direct complication attributed to JJ stents, whose common complications are infection, hematuria, and irritative/positional flank pain.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a side effect of anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) medications used for overactive bladder?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation, not diarrhea, along with dry mouth, blurred vision, and confusion, due to inhibition of parasympathetic (muscarinic) activity on the gut and other organs.

questions.text: A fetus is found to have antenatal hydronephrosis on prenatal ultrasound. Appropriate postnatal evaluation includes:
options: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
originalOptions: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
questions.correctAnswer: A) Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
questions.correctAnswerText: Renal ultrasound with VCUG and/or renal scan depending on severity
questions.explanation: Postnatal workup of antenatal hydronephrosis is guided by severity, using renal ultrasound as the initial test, followed by VCUG (to assess for reflux) and/or renal scan (to assess function/obstruction) as indicated.

questions.text: A pregnant woman is found to have mild hydronephrosis on ultrasound with no symptoms of infection or stone disease. This is most likely explained by:
options: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
originalOptions: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
questions.correctAnswer: C) Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
questions.correctAnswerText: Compression of the ureter by the gravid uterus (physiological hydronephrosis)
questions.explanation: Mild hydronephrosis in pregnancy, particularly on the right side, is commonly physiological due to compression of the ureter by the enlarging gravid uterus and does not necessarily indicate pathology.

allQuestions.explanation: Parasympathetic fibers from S2–S4 release nitric oxide, which raises cGMP and relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle, producing tumescence; sympathetic (thoracolumbar) outflow instead causes detumescence.

options: Needle injury to the cavernosal artery
originalOptions: Needle injury to the cavernosal artery
allQuestions.explanation: Non-ischemic priapism results from an arterio-sinusoidal fistula, classically from trauma, needle injury, or iatrogenic penile surgery; neurologic shock is instead a recognized cause of ischemic (low-flow) priapism.

allQuestions.text: Which condition is characteristically associated with subcutaneous wire/device erosion through the skin?
allQuestions.explanation: Erosion of the implanted device or its components through the overlying skin is a recognized mechanical complication of penile prosthesis surgery.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following antihypertensive drugs negatively affects erectile function?
allQuestions.explanation: Thiazide diuretics (Hydrochlorothiazide) are reported to cause ED, while alpha-blockers (terazosin) and ARBs (losartan) tend to improve sexual function, and amlodipine/captopril are not associated with worsening erectile function.

allQuestions.text: Which characteristic is typically associated with organic ED, in contrast to psychogenic ED?
options: Presence of an identifiable interpersonal relationship factor
originalOptions: Presence of an identifiable interpersonal relationship factor
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Gradual decline in erectile ability
allQuestions.explanation: Organic ED typically has a progressive, gradual course, whereas sudden onset, situational occurrence, and preserved morning/nocturnal erections all favor a psychogenic cause.

allQuestions.text: During a rigid erection, all of the following are true EXCEPT:

Corporal pressure rises to several hundred millimeters of mercury

allQuestions.text: A quadriplegic patient presents with priapism. Corporeal blood gas analysis reveals PO2 = 94, PCO2 = 37, pH = 7.4. He was previously treated with intracavernosal phenylephrine without improvement. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
allQuestions.explanation: A near-normal blood gas indicates non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism, which is managed conservatively and, if intervention is required, by selective arterial embolization rather than aspiration or agents used for ischemic priapism.

allQuestions.text: In ischemic priapism, which of the following is typically absent?
allQuestions.explanation: Ischemic (low-flow) priapism is characterized by absent or markedly reduced arterial inflow to the cavernosal artery on Doppler, with a painful, fully rigid erection.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a psychogenic cause of erectile dysfunction?
allQuestions.explanation: Anxiety acts through overinhibition of the spinal erection center and excessive sympathetic outflow, making it a psychogenic cause, while the other options are organic/structural causes of ED.

allQuestions.text: Pain in the flaccid penis is usually due to:
options: A calculus impacted in the distal ureter
originalOptions: A calculus impacted in the distal ureter
allQuestions.explanation: Pain in the flaccid penis typically reflects bladder or urethral inflammation (or paraphimosis), whereas Peyronie's disease and priapism classically cause pain in the erect penis.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are characteristics of psychogenic ED EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: A gradual, progressive decline in erectile function is characteristic of organic ED, whereas sudden onset, situational occurrence, and preserved nocturnal erections point to a psychogenic cause.

allQuestions.text: What will penile Doppler ultrasound show in a case of ischemic priapism?
options: Increased venous outflow from the corpora
Increased arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery

Increased arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Decreased or absent arterial inflow in the cavernous artery
allQuestions.explanation: Ischemic priapism is a low-flow state, so Doppler characteristically shows absent or minimal arterial inflow into the cavernosal artery.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with priapism of 2 weeks' duration; corporeal blood gas shows PO2 > 90, PCO2 < 30. What is the best management?
allQuestions.explanation: A high PO2 and low PCO2 indicate non-ischemic (high-flow) priapism, which, when intervention is required, is managed with selective arterial embolization rather than aspiration or sympathomimetic injection, which are used for ischemic priapism.

allQuestions.text: An 80-year-old paraplegic man develops a prolonged, painful erection after an intracorporeal injection given to treat erectile dysfunction. Which intracorporeal drug should be given to relieve him?
allQuestions.explanation: This describes ischemic priapism following intracavernosal injection therapy, which is treated with aspiration/irrigation followed by intracavernosal phenylephrine (an alpha-agonist); alprostadil, papaverine, and sildenafil are used to induce erection, not to treat priapism.

allQuestions.text: A 38-year-old paraplegic man develops a sustained erection lasting 10 hours following intracorporeal injection of 10 mcg of prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil). What is the most appropriate management?
allQuestions.explanation: This is drug-induced ischemic priapism, which is treated with corporal aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine, an alpha-agonist that induces vasoconstriction and detumescence.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements about phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors is TRUE?

allQuestions.text: Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors increase the cytoplasmic concentration of:
allQuestions.explanation: PDE5 inhibitors block the breakdown of cGMP by phosphodiesterase type 5, prolonging cGMP-mediated cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation.

allQuestions.text: An elderly patient on nitroglycerin presents with erectile dysfunction. What is the most appropriate treatment?
allQuestions.explanation: PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrate use due to the risk of severe hypotension, so a non-pharmacologic option such as a vacuum erection device is appropriate; testosterone and tamsulosin are not indicated without evidence of hypogonadism or BPH.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a recognized hormonal cause of erectile dysfunction?
allQuestions.explanation: Both hypogonadism (low testosterone) and hyperprolactinemia are established hormonal causes of ED; hyperprolactinemia additionally suppresses GnRH, which further lowers testosterone.

allQuestions.text: What is the mechanism of action of PDE5 inhibitors in the treatment of erectile dysfunction?
options: They increase cAMP by inhibiting adenylate cyclase breakdown

They prevent breakdown of cGMP, prolonging cavernosal smooth muscle relaxation
They block alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in the prostate and bladder neck

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes true hematuria from hemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria?
allQuestions.explanation: Dipstick is positive for blood in all three conditions, but only true hematuria shows intact red blood cells on microscopic urinalysis.

allQuestions.text: A patient reports blood appearing only at the very end of the urinary stream, after most of the urine has already passed. This pattern of terminal hematuria most suggests pathology arising from:
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Bladder neck or prostatic inflammation
allQuestions.explanation: Initial hematuria localizes to the urethra, total hematuria to the bladder or upper tract, and terminal hematuria to the bladder neck or prostatic urethra.

allQuestions.text: A 68-year-old smoker presents with a single episode of painless gross hematuria. Which diagnosis must be excluded first as the classic cause of painless gross hematuria in a patient over 50 years old?
allQuestions.explanation: Painless gross hematuria in a patient over 50 is bladder cancer until proven otherwise, warranting cystoscopy and upper tract imaging regardless of other findings.

allQuestions.text: A normotensive patient is found to have isolated microscopic hematuria on routine urinalysis, with no other urinary symptoms and a normal examination. What is the most appropriate initial action?
allQuestions.explanation: Isolated, asymptomatic microscopic hematuria in a low-risk patient is initially managed conservatively with a repeat urinalysis rather than immediate invasive workup.

allQuestions.text: When taking a history from a patient presenting with hematuria, which combination of questions is most important to ask?
allQuestions.explanation: Onset, presence of clots, and timing during the urinary stream all help localize the source and severity of hematuria, so all should be asked.

allQuestions.text: Hematuria in an adult should be treated as a warning sign of which of the following until proven otherwise?
allQuestions.explanation: Although hematuria has many causes, it is classically taught that hematuria in an adult signals malignancy, most often bladder cancer, until excluded.

allQuestions.text: A 70-year-old male smoker presents with gross hematuria persisting for 3 months. What is the most appropriate next step in investigation?
allQuestions.explanation: Persistent gross hematuria in an older smoker requires full evaluation of both the upper tract (CT urogram) and lower tract (cystoscopy) to exclude urothelial malignancy.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following best defines stress urinary incontinence?
options: Involuntary leakage preceded by a sudden urge to void
Continuous leakage of urine unrelated to activity
Leakage of urine that occurs only during sleep
Leakage of urine following bladder overdistension
Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing

allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Involuntary leakage of urine associated with effort, exertion, coughing, or sneezing
allQuestions.explanation: Stress incontinence occurs when rises in intra-abdominal pressure overcome urethral resistance, typically from pelvic floor weakness or sphincteric incompetence.

allQuestions.text: A patient with overactive bladder and urgency incontinence is being started on treatment. Which type of incontinence is most often managed pharmacologically as first-line therapy?
allQuestions.explanation: Urge incontinence from detrusor overactivity responds well to antimuscarinics or beta-3 agonists (mirabegron), unlike stress incontinence, which is managed primarily with conservative or surgical measures.

allQuestions.text: A 48-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presents with urine leakage on coughing and sneezing. What is the most appropriate initial management?
allQuestions.explanation: Conservative pelvic floor exercises (at least 8 contractions, 3 times daily for 3 months) are first-line before considering surgical options such as slings or Burch colposuspension.

allQuestions.text: A 43-year-old woman develops constant urinary leakage 7 days after hysterectomy, not aggravated by coughing and without associated urgency. What is the most likely underlying cause?
allQuestions.explanation: Continuous, position-independent leakage after pelvic surgery strongly suggests an iatrogenic vesicovaginal fistula creating a direct communication between bladder and vagina.

allQuestions.text: Continuous incontinence, defined as leakage of urine at all times and in all positions, is most commonly caused by which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: A fistulous communication between the bladder and vagina bypasses the normal continence mechanism entirely, producing constant leakage regardless of posture or activity.

allQuestions.text: In female patients, an ectopic ureter classically causes continuous urinary incontinence because the ureter inserts:
options: Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
originalOptions: Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Distal to the external urethral sphincter (e.g., vagina or vestibule)
allQuestions.explanation: In females, an ectopic ureter frequently opens below the external sphincter, bypassing continence mechanisms; in males it opens above the sphincter and instead causes recurrent UTIs rather than incontinence.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT considered a risk factor for urinary incontinence?
allQuestions.explanation: Female sex, not male sex, is a recognized risk factor for urinary incontinence due to a shorter urethra and the effects of pregnancy and childbirth on pelvic floor support.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor specifically for stress urinary incontinence?
allQuestions.explanation: Vaginal childbirth weakens pelvic floor support and increases SUI risk, whereas nulliparous women have a comparatively lower risk.

allQuestions.text: Which class of medication should be avoided when treating stress urinary incontinence in a male patient?
allQuestions.explanation: Anticholinergics target detrusor overactivity in urge incontinence and have no role in stress incontinence, which in men is usually secondary to sphincter injury after prostate surgery.

allQuestions.text: What is the most common overall indication for placement of an indwelling Foley catheter?

allQuestions.text: A patient started on an antimuscarinic for urge incontinence develops several adverse effects. Which of the following is NOT typically caused by anticholinergic medications?
allQuestions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation, not diarrhea, along with dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, and confusion.

allQuestions.text: Before initiating mirabegron for urge incontinence, which of the following should prompt the greatest caution or avoidance of therapy?
allQuestions.explanation: Mirabegron can raise blood pressure, so severe uncontrolled hypertension is a major safety concern, whereas significant urinary retention with high PVR is a relative caution rather than the primary contraindication.

allQuestions.text: During cystometry, a patient's intravesical pressure (Pves) is 45 cmH2O and abdominal pressure (Pabd) is 15 cmH2O. What is the calculated detrusor pressure (Pdet)?
allQuestions.explanation: Detrusor pressure is calculated as Pdet = Pves − Pabd, so 45 − 15 = 30 cmH2O.

allQuestions.text: A 6-year-old child is undergoing urodynamic evaluation. Using the standard pediatric formula, what is the expected bladder capacity?
allQuestions.explanation: Pediatric bladder capacity is estimated as (Age + 2) × 30 mL; for a 6-year-old this is (6+2) × 30 = 240 mL.

allQuestions.text: Before initiating mirabegron for the treatment of urge urinary incontinence, which of the following conditions is the most appropriate reason to avoid or use the drug with significant caution?
options: Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual
originalOptions: Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Significant urinary retention with high post-void residual

allQuestions.explanation: Mirabegron (a β3-adrenergic agonist) relaxes the detrusor muscle during bladder filling, which may worsen pre-existing urinary retention. Therefore, patients with significant urinary retention and a high post-void residual should generally avoid the drug or receive it only with careful monitoring. Dysuria, kidney stones, and hematuria are not contraindications by themselves.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following syndromes represents the most common chromosomal cause of male infertility?
allQuestions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common chromosomal abnormality causing male infertility by leading to primary testicular failure and azoospermia, whereas Kallmann syndrome is a genetic hormone disorder (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) rather than a chromosomal aneuploidy, Turner syndrome exclusively affects females (45,X), and Noonan syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic condition not characterized by a chromosomal number defect.

allQuestions.text: What is the first-line investigation of choice for a male presenting with infertility?
allQuestions.explanation: Semen analysis (seminal fluid analysis) is the first-line investigation in male infertility, assessing volume, sperm concentration, motility, and morphology; hormonal testing, ultrasound, and karyotyping are reserved for further work-up based on initial findings.

allQuestions.text: Infertility in males with cystic fibrosis is most commonly caused by which of the following?

allQuestions.explanation: CFTR gene mutations in cystic fibrosis lead to CBAVD; spermatogenesis is normal, but the resulting obstructive azoospermia causes infertility.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is the primary inhibitor of LH release from the anterior pituitary?
allQuestions.explanation: Testosterone provides negative feedback on both the hypothalamus (↓GnRH) and pituitary (↓LH). Inhibin B, secreted by Sertoli cells, selectively inhibits FSH rather than LH.

allQuestions.text: Teratospermia refers to which of the following semen abnormalities?

allQuestions.explanation: Teratospermia: sperm morphology below the lower reference limit of normal forms (WHO lower limit ~4% normal forms) , A: Azoospermia , B: Asthenospermia , C: Oligospermia .

allQuestions.text: The majority of seminal fluid volume is contributed by which structure?
allQuestions.explanation: The seminal vesicles contribute the majority of seminal fluid volume, while the prostate contributes about 1/6, and sperm contribute only about 1%.

allQuestions.text: At which life stages do the major physiological peaks of testosterone production occur in males?

allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Embryonic (fetal) development, the neonatal period, and puberty
allQuestions.explanation: Testosterone peaks at three distinct life stages: embryonic development, the first few months of neonatal life (mini-puberty), and puberty — driving prostatic and genital development at each stage.

allQuestions.text: A young male bodybuilder using exogenous testosterone is most likely to experience which effect on his fertility?
options: Increased fertility due to higher androgen levels
Decreased fertility due to suppression of pituitary FSH and LH
Fertility effects depend only on the route of administration
originalOptions: Increased fertility due to higher androgen levels
Decreased fertility due to suppression of pituitary FSH and LH
Fertility effects depend only on the route of administration
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Decreased fertility due to suppression of pituitary FSH and LH
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Decreased fertility due to suppression of pituitary FSH and LH
allQuestions.explanation: Exogenous testosterone suppresses hypothalamic-pituitary GnRH/FSH/LH secretion via negative feedback, lowering intratesticular testosterone and impairing spermatogenesis, unlike endogenous testicular testosterone.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with infertility, small testes, azoospermia, and an elevated FSH level. This clinical picture is most consistent with which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: Small testes, azoospermia, and elevated FSH indicate primary testicular failure (which is synonymous with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) ; hypogonadotropic hypogonadism instead presents with low FSH/LH , and obstructive azoospermia typically has a normal FSH.

allQuestions.text: In a patient with azoospermia, which hormone finding suggests an obstructive cause rather than testicular failure?
allQuestions.explanation: Obstructive azoospermia typically shows a normal FSH because spermatogenesis is intact, whereas non-obstructive azoospermia (testicular failure) shows an elevated FSH due to loss of Sertoli cell inhibin feedback.

allQuestions.text: The anatomical basis of the blood-testis barrier is formed by which of the following?
options: The basement membrane of the seminiferous tubule
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
originalOptions: The basement membrane of the seminiferous tubule
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
allQuestions.explanation: Sertoli cells are linked by tight junctions that form the blood-testis barrier, creating an immunologically privileged compartment for developing sperm, which form only after puberty.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a recognized complication of cryptorchidism?
allQuestions.explanation: Cryptorchidism impairs fertility due to an unfavorable thermal environment for spermatogenesis; it also raises the risk of testicular (not bladder) cancer.

allQuestions.text: What is the karyotype of Klinefelter syndrome?
allQuestions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is caused by an extra X chromosome (47,XXY), resulting in small firm testes, gynecomastia, tall stature, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism with infertility.

allQuestions.text: Infertility is defined as the failure of a couple to achieve pregnancy after which duration of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse?
allQuestions.explanation: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after 12 months of regular, unprotected intercourse; shorter periods (3–6 months) are not sufficient to establish the diagnosis since most couples conceive within a year.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following pairs correctly represents the prevalence of varicocele in the general male population versus in infertile men?
allQuestions.explanation: Varicocele affects about 15% of the general male population but is found in roughly 35–40% of infertile men, and is even more common in men with secondary infertility.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is considered a favorable prognostic factor in male infertility?
options: Absence of previous pregnancy with the same partner
originalOptions: Absence of previous pregnancy with the same partner
allQuestions.explanation: A shorter duration of infertility, younger female partner age, and a history of previous conception are all favorable prognostic factors; the opposite findings (long duration, older maternal age, no prior pregnancy) indicate a poorer prognosis.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are recognized categories of causes of male infertility EXCEPT:
options: Testicular causes (e.g., varicocele, cryptorchidism, Klinefelter syndrome)
Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
originalOptions: Testicular causes (e.g., varicocele, cryptorchidism, Klinefelter syndrome)
Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Purely psychological causes unrelated to any organic pathology
allQuestions.explanation: Male infertility is classified into pre-testicular, testicular, post-testicular, and idiopathic causes; a purely psychological category unrelated to organic pathology is not part of this recognized classification.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are recognized causes of obstructive azoospermia EXCEPT:
options: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
originalOptions: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens
allQuestions.explanation: CBAVD, vasectomy, post-infectious epididymal obstruction, and ejaculatory duct obstruction are classic causes of obstructive azoospermia with preserved spermatogenesis; Klinefelter syndrome causes non-obstructive (testicular failure) azoospermia due to primary testicular failure, not obstruction.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements regarding semen fluid analysis in obstructive azoospermia is correct?
options: Typical obstructive azoospermia shows no sperm with usually normal semen volume; ejaculatory duct obstruction specifically shows low volume with acidic, low-fructose semen

Both typical obstructive azoospermia and ejaculatory duct obstruction show normal semen volume and normal fructose

Typical obstructive azoospermia shows no sperm with low semen volume; ejaculatory duct obstruction shows normal volume with normal fructose
Both typical obstructive azoospermia and ejaculatory duct obstruction show low semen volume and low fructose

allQuestions.explanation: In general, obstructive azoospermia preserves normal ejaculate volume since spermatogenesis is intact; however, ejaculatory duct obstruction or absent seminal vesicles is an important exception producing low-volume, acidic, low-fructose semen, and FSH remains normal since testicular function is preserved.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following pairs represents andrological conditions correctly associated with varicocele?
allQuestions.explanation: Varicocele is classically associated with male infertility (abnormal semen parameters) and testicular hypotrophy/atrophy due to impaired thermoregulation and venous stasis; the other listed pairings are unrelated conditions not causally linked to varicocele.

allQuestions.text: A young infertile male undergoes karyotype analysis. Which of the following is the most common genetic cause of male infertility?
allQuestions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is the most common sex chromosome abnormality and genetic cause of male infertility, presenting with small firm testes, azoospermia, and elevated FSH/LH with low testosterone.

allQuestions.text: During TURP, a patient develops confusion, nausea, bradycardia, and hypertension near the end of a prolonged resection. Serum sodium is low. This is best explained by:
options: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia

allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Absorption of hypotonic irrigating fluid causing dilutional hyponatremia
allQuestions.explanation: TUR syndrome results from absorption of hypotonic irrigating solution through open venous sinuses during resection, causing hypervolemic hyponatremia with confusion, bradycardia, hypertension, and visual disturbances.

allQuestions.text: Which factor is most associated with increased risk of TUR syndrome?
options: Use of bipolar resection with saline irrigation
originalOptions: Use of bipolar resection with saline irrigation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Resection time greater than 90 minutes
allQuestions.explanation: TUR syndrome risk increases with resection times exceeding 90 minutes and is more common in older men; bipolar TURP performed under saline (isotonic) irrigation reduces this risk.

allQuestions.text: A patient requires long-term indwelling catheterization. Compared to latex, silicone catheters are preferred because they:
options: Are only available in smaller sizes
originalOptions: Are only available in smaller sizes
allQuestions.explanation: Silicone catheters induce less tissue inflammation than latex, making them preferable for long-term catheterization, despite latex being cheaper and more widely available.

allQuestions.text: A 24 French Foley catheter has an outer diameter of approximately:
allQuestions.explanation: Catheter French size divided by 3 gives the outer diameter in millimeters; 24 ÷ 3 = 8 mm.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a recognized indication for urethral catheterization?

Suspected urethral injury with blood at the meatus
High-riding prostate on rectal exam after trauma
Pelvic fracture with suspected urethral disruption

Suspected urethral injury with blood at the meatus
High-riding prostate on rectal exam after trauma
Pelvic fracture with suspected urethral disruption

allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Monitoring urine output in a critically ill patient
allQuestions.explanation: Monitoring urine output is a standard, common indication for catheterization. Suspected urethral injury (blood at meatus, high-riding prostate, pelvic fracture with urethral disruption) is a contraindication until imaging excludes injury.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to transurethral Foley catheter placement?
options: Need for a clean urine sample
originalOptions: Need for a clean urine sample
allQuestions.explanation: Suspected urethral injury is a contraindication to urethral catheterization; a retrograde urethrogram should be performed first, and a suprapubic catheter used if drainage is needed.

allQuestions.text: Chronic urinary retention is best distinguished from acute retention by which feature?
options: Sudden onset of severe suprapubic pain
Rapid resolution with a single catheterization
originalOptions: Sudden onset of severe suprapubic pain
Rapid resolution with a single catheterization

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized complication of long-term double-J (JJ) ureteral stenting?
allQuestions.explanation: Long-standing catheters (not JJ stents specifically) are linked to stone formation and bladder cancer risk with prolonged indwelling urethral catheters; urothelial cancer is not a typical direct complication attributed to JJ stents, whose common complications are infection, hematuria, and irritative/positional flank pain.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a side effect of anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) medications used for overactive bladder?
allQuestions.explanation: Anticholinergics cause constipation, not diarrhea, along with dry mouth, blurred vision, and confusion, due to inhibition of parasympathetic (muscarinic) activity on the gut and other organs.
